title: Textos — apropiate de uno y exponelo
goals: Elegí un texto, estudialo a fondo y aprendé a hablar de él: explicarlo, exponerlo, responder preguntas e improvisar.
El Texto 1 (termodinámica y entropía) está desarrollado a fondo: es el que se prepara para exponer.
Los Textos 2, 3 y 4 están presentes para leerlos y escucharlos, con una capa mínima de práctica.

source.note: Narrativa nuestra de comprensión auditiva sobre el tema del texto.

atoms.narrative: Imagine you drop a little milk into a cup of black tea. At first you can see it clearly: a white cloud in a dark liquid. If you wait, the milk spreads out and the tea becomes one uniform colour. You never see the opposite happen. The milk does not gather itself back into a cloud, even though nothing in the first law forbids it. The reason is entropy: there are far more ways for the molecules to be mixed than for them to be separated, so the mixed state is overwhelmingly more likely.
atoms.speaker: narrator

questions.q: What happens to the milk if you wait?
accept: the tea becomes one uniform colour

questions.q: Does the milk ever gather itself back into a cloud?
Why is the mixed state more likely?
accept: because there are more ways to be mixed
there are far more ways for the molecules to be mixed

source.note: Narrativa nuestra de comprensión auditiva sobre el tema del texto.

atoms.narrative: Imagine you record a short film of a cup falling from a table and breaking on the floor. If you play the film backwards, everybody laughs, because broken pieces never jump back onto the table and become a cup again. Now imagine a film of two billiard balls hitting each other. Played backwards, that film looks perfectly normal. The laws for two balls work in both directions of time. But when there are many, many parts, one direction becomes overwhelmingly more likely than the other. This is why some physicists say that entropy gives us the arrow of time.
atoms.speaker: narrator

questions.q: What happens if you play the film of the falling cup backwards?
Does the film of two billiard balls look normal backwards?

atoms.prompt: Explain the concept of entropy as described in the text.
atoms.modelAnswer: Entropy is a way of counting arrangements. A cup of tea is made up of many, many molecules in random motion, and we never see them one by one. If we re-arranged them slightly, the tea would look much the same to us. Loosely speaking, the entropy of the cup counts the number of ways in which you could arrange the molecules and still leave the cup looking the same macroscopically. It is defined in the same way for any system made up of microscopic parts, and there is even a relatively simple formula to calculate it. The second law adds that the entropy of an isolated system will tend to increase over time.
modelVariants: Entropy measures how many microscopic arrangements give you the same thing at our scale. In a cup of tea there are many, many molecules moving at random. We cannot see them, so a small re-arrangement would look identical to us. Entropy counts those identical-looking arrangements. The same definition works for any system made of microscopic parts, and the second law says that in an isolated system entropy tends to grow until it reaches a maximum.

Think of a cup of tea. It contains an enormous number of molecules in random motion, and we only see the tea, not the molecules. Many different arrangements of those molecules look exactly the same to us. Entropy is the count of those arrangements. Because there are far more disordered arrangements than ordered ones, an isolated system left alone will tend towards higher entropy.

Generalizá: vale para cualquier sistema de partes microscópicas.

atoms.prompt: Give a one to two minute presentation about the text 'Tea and nineteenth century physics'.
atoms.modelAnswer: I choose text 1, 'Tea and nineteenth century physics', by Hannah Darken. First, the everyday fact. If you leave a hot cup of tea on a table, it always cools down. It never becomes hotter. Everybody knows this, but behind it there is a whole area of physics: thermodynamics, the theory of heat and heat flow. It was developed mostly during the nineteenth century. Before we see the laws, we need to look at two ideas. The first idea is temperature. Temperature is not a thing inside the tea. It is a bulk property of molecules and atoms in motion. Atoms that move fast produce a warm temperature. Atoms that move very little produce a cold one. The second idea is entropy. Tea is made of many, many molecules in random motion, and we never see them. If we re-arranged them slightly, the tea would look the same to us. So entropy counts the number of ways we could arrange the molecules and still see the same cup of tea. Now, the text gives four laws. The zeroth law: if two systems are in thermal equilibrium with a third one, they are in equilibrium with each other. The first law: energy cannot be created or destroyed, only transferred. The second law: in an isolated system, entropy tends to increase over time. The third law: at absolute zero, entropy reaches a constant minimum. In the end, my cold cup of tea is the second law in action. And the same theory explains weather forecasting, planets and moons, and even black holes.
modelVariants: The text is called 'Tea and nineteenth century physics' and it was written by Hannah Darken for plus.maths.org. It uses a very ordinary situation, a cup of tea going cold, to introduce thermodynamics. Thermodynamics is the theory of heat and heat flow, and it was developed mostly during the nineteenth century, when it was discovered that temperature is a bulk property of molecules and atoms in motion. Atoms that move around fast produce a warm temperature, and colder temperatures come from atoms that move very little. The text then introduces entropy, which counts the number of ways you could arrange the molecules and still see the same cup of tea. Finally it lists the four laws of thermodynamics, and it ends by saying that thermodynamics plays a part in weather forecasting, in planets and moons, and even in black holes.

5. Primera idea — temperatura: no es una cosa, es movimiento (rápido/lento).
6. Segunda idea — entropía: contar ordenamientos que se ven igual.
7. ANUNCIO: «ahora, las cuatro leyes» (cero, primera, segunda, tercera).
8. Cierre: mi taza fría ES la segunda ley, y hasta dónde llega la teoría.

atoms.prompt: Explain the four laws of thermodynamics in your own words.
atoms.modelAnswer: The zeroth law says that if two systems are in thermal equilibrium with a third one, they are also in thermal equilibrium with each other. The first law says that energy cannot be created or destroyed: it can only change form or be transferred from one object to another. The second law says that the entropy of an isolated system not in equilibrium will tend to increase over time, approaching a maximum value. The third law says that as temperature approaches absolute zero, the entropy of a system approaches a constant minimum.
modelVariants: There are four. The zeroth one connects three systems: if two of them are in equilibrium with a third, they are in equilibrium with each other. The first one says energy is conserved; it only changes form or moves. The second one says entropy grows in an isolated system until it reaches a maximum. The third one says that at absolute zero the entropy reaches a constant minimum.

atoms.prompt: Explain to a friend who has never studied physics why a hot cup of tea always gets cold.
atoms.modelAnswer: Think about what temperature really is. It is not a thing inside the tea; it is how fast the molecules are moving. In hot tea they move fast, and in the cold air of the room they move more slowly. When the cup touches the air and the table, the fast molecules push the slow ones, and energy passes from the tea to the room. That energy is never destroyed, it only moves. It keeps moving until both are at the same temperature, and then we say they are in thermal equilibrium. That is why the tea always gets cold, and never hot.
modelVariants: Temperature is really about movement: fast molecules feel hot, slow molecules feel cold. Your tea is full of fast molecules and the room is full of slow ones, so energy leaks from the cup to the room until they match. Nothing is lost, it just moves. And it only goes one way, because there are many more ways for the energy to be spread out than concentrated in the cup.

atoms.prompt: Give your opinion: does it help to explain physics with everyday objects like a cup of tea?
atoms.modelAnswer: In my opinion it helps a lot, at least at the beginning. A cup of tea is something everybody has seen, so the reader starts from a real image instead of an abstract definition. In this text the same cup explains three different things: heat flow, temperature as movement, and entropy. That economy is what makes the example good. I also think there is a risk, because an everyday image can hide the mathematics. The text is honest about that: it says there is a relatively simple formula to calculate entropy, so the reader knows that the real definition is a formula and not a cup of tea.
modelVariants: I think everyday examples are useful because they give you something to picture. Here the cup of tea carries the whole text: it explains cooling, temperature and entropy. But an example is not a definition, and the author knows it, because she mentions that there is a formula behind the idea.

atoms.title: Tea and nineteenth century physics
atoms.speaker: narrator

blocks.text: As I sadly drink my now-cold cup of tea, I can cheer myself up with the fascinating area of physics known as thermodynamics. Everyone knows that if you leave a hot cup of tea sitting on a table, or indeed leave any object in cooler surroundings, it will inevitably cool down. Thermodynamics, the theory of heat and heat flow, was developed mostly during the 19th century when it was discovered that temperature is a bulk property of molecules and atoms in motion. Atoms that move around fast, as they do in a hot cup of tea, produce a warm temperature. Colder temperatures come from atoms that move very little, as is the case in a rigidly frozen block of ice tea.

An important concept in this context is that of entropy. This can again be illustrated using tea, which is made up of many, many molecules in random motion. We don't see those molecules, in fact, the tea would look much the same to us if we re-arranged them slightly. Loosely speaking, the entropy of the cup of tea counts the number of ways in which you could arrange the molecules that would leave the cup of tea looking the same macroscopically. It's defined in the same way for any other system made up of microscopic parts, and there even is a relatively simple formula that tells you how to calculate it.
There are four fundamental laws of thermodynamics:

items: Zeroth law: If two systems are in thermal equilibrium with a third system, they are in thermal equilibrium with each other. Two systems are in thermal equilibrium if, when they are connected by something that can transfer heat, there isn't any net flow of heat energy between them.
First law: Energy cannot be created or destroyed. It can only change form or be transferred from one object to another.
Second law: The entropy of an isolated system not in equilibrium will tend to increase over time, approaching a maximum value at equilibrium.
Third law: As temperature approaches absolute zero, the lowest theoretically possible temperature, the entropy of a system approaches a constant minimum.

blocks.text: Thermodynamics plays a part anywhere where temperature, heat, work and energy are involved, so it's not so surprising to see it plays a role in weather forecasting and the evolution of planets, moons and even black holes. But that is not all: Thermodynamics has also led to new ways to approach fundamental questions about understanding information, time and life.

atoms.title: Maths that will help you as an adult: from baking a cake to asking for a pay rise
atoms.speaker: narrator

blocks.text: The UK's Prime Minister Rishi Sunak has proposed that school pupils should continue learning maths until 18. He argues that students need numeracy skills for careers and adult life. But what about adults who already feel anxious when they see numbers? Millions of people in the UK struggle with basic arithmetic, and many suffer from maths anxiety.
Still, maths can help us make better decisions in daily life. Here are some examples.

sections.heading: 1. Use ratios to adapt a recipe

blocks.text: Imagine you find a recipe for four people, but you are cooking for three. Ratios can help. A ratio compares parts. If the recipe calls for four parts, you only need three.

For example, if the recipe needs 120g of flour, divide by four to find one part: 30g. Multiply by three people: 90g of flour. If the recipe says six teaspoons of oil, divide by four (1.5 teaspoons). Multiply by three: 4.5 teaspoons.

sections.heading: 2. Understand averages to check your salary

blocks.text: In 2021, the average yearly earnings for full-time workers in the UK was £38,131. This number is the mean: all salaries added together, divided by the number of workers. But the mean can be misleading. A few very high salaries can raise the mean, even if most people earn less.

Another type of average is the median. Imagine lining up all workers from the lowest salary to the highest. The person in the middle represents the median. In 2021, the median salary was £31,285. This number is often more useful, because it shows what a "typical" worker earns.
If your salary is much lower than the median in your field, it may be worth asking why.
Phones make splitting the bill easy, but sometimes your battery is dead. Quick division skills are useful.
Suppose the bill is £92 for four people. Round up to £100: 100 ÷ 4 = 25. But the real bill is £8 less. £8 ÷ 4 = £2. So each pays £25 − £2 = £23.
Another method: round down to £80. That makes £20 each. Then divide the remaining £12 by four: £3 each. Total: £23.

sections.heading: 4. Plan a hike with Naismith's rule

blocks.text: Maths can even help outdoors. A Scottish mountaineer created Naismith's rule: allow one hour for each 5km walked, plus ten minutes for every 100m climbed.

If your route is 15km with 600m of climbing, that is three hours for distance plus one hour for climbing: four hours total. Add time for breaks, lunch, or a slower pace, and you might plan six hours. Maths helps you set a safe starting time.

Maths is not only for school or careers. It is a tool for everyday life: cooking, understanding salaries, paying bills, or planning trips. With the right mindset, everyone can learn to use maths more confidently.

atoms.title: How Many Yottabytes in a Quettabyte? Extreme Numbers Get New Names
atoms.speaker: narrator

sections.heading: New prefixes for huge and tiny numbers

blocks.text: By the 2030s, the world will generate around a yottabyte of data per year. That's an enormous number, enough DVDs stacked all the way to Mars. To keep up with this growth, scientists have agreed on new prefixes in the metric system to describe extremely large and extremely small quantities.
On 18 November, representatives from governments worldwide met at the General Conference on Weights and Measures near Paris. They voted to add four new prefixes to the International System of Units.

items: ronto, ten to the minus twenty-seventh
quecto, ten to the minus thirtieth

blocks.text: For example, Earth weighs about one ronnagram, and the mass of an electron is about one quectogram.
This was the first update since 1991, when prefixes like zetta, yocto, yotta and zepto were introduced. At that time, chemists wanted terms to express numbers close to Avogadro's constant.

Today, the main driver is data science. Richard Brown, a metrologist at the UK National Physical Laboratory, worked for five years on the proposal. With global data already measured in zettabytes, people had begun using unofficial names like hella or bronto. Even Google's converter showed "hellabyte."

Brown explained that these terms were problematic because their symbols are already used in the metric system. For example, h stands for hecto and H is the unit of inductance, the henry. To avoid confusion, official new names were needed.
Brown looked for letters not already used in SI symbols. The choices were r and q. Following tradition, large prefixes end in "a", like mega or tera, while small ones end in "o", like nano or atto.
The sounds also connect to Greek or Latin numbers: ronna resembles ennea, nine, and quetta resembles deka, ten. One suggestion, quecca, was rejected because it sounded like a Portuguese swear word.

Experts welcomed the change. Georgette Macdonald, director of Canada's Metrology Research Centre, said the new prefixes provide consistency and avoid confusion. Even though science mostly needs large prefixes now, adding small ones keeps the system balanced.
Olivier Pellegrino, a metrologist in Portugal, noted that names like giga and tera once sounded strange too. With use, ronna and quetta will feel normal.

Brown pointed out that no letters remain unused in the alphabet for future prefixes. If science ever needs terms beyond ten to the thirty-third, one option could be compound prefixes, like kiloquetta. But for now, scientists can always use powers of ten.
After years of effort to get approval, Brown said he hasn't yet imagined the new terms in everyday use. "It will be absolutely fantastic," he added.

atoms.title: What Professional Development for Math Teachers Should Look Like
atoms.speaker: narrator

blocks.text: Tonya Clarke's vision for math instruction in Clayton County public schools sounds simple: she wants students to think, reason, and analyze in order to solve real-world problems. But putting that vision into practice is more complicated.
It requires teachers to plan differently, giving students opportunities to problem-solve, discuss strategies, and work on project-based learning.

One key part of this change has been the creation of math ambassadors: teachers who receive special training from the district and then mentor other teachers in their schools. Clarke, the district's K-12 math coordinator, explained how this works.

How do you help teachers learn to support problem-solving? The ambassadors provide job-embedded support. They brainstorm strategies, practice them, and then bring ideas back to their schools. This way, they can lead collaborative planning sessions and help colleagues design more meaningful projects.

Does what teachers need vary by school? Yes. Each school has a personalized improvement plan. At the start of the year, Clarke's team meets with administrators and teachers to set goals. Some schools receive weekly visits, others every two weeks, and some only occasional support through virtual meetings or lead teachers.

What challenges remain? Clarke admits that student scores are not yet showing the desired results. The district is working to connect instruction with leadership, ensuring that strategies are implemented consistently.
Ambassadors can prepare teachers for collaborative planning, but if schools lack structures to protect planning time, the work cannot be fully realized.

What advice would you give to other districts? Clarke suggests breaking training into smaller groups instead of trying to train everyone at once. She also encourages collaboration with other departments.

For example, she worked with the English Language Arts department to improve how math teachers teach vocabulary. Many secondary math teachers are not trained in language development, so they needed support to help struggling readers. Clarke's team learned techniques from reading instruction to help students decode passages and understand math problems.

Clarke's approach shows that changing math instruction is not only about new methods in the classroom. It requires mentoring, collaboration, personalized plans, and cross-department teamwork. The goal is clear: to help students become confident problem-solvers who can apply math in real life.
